name: Splits
seoDesc: Splits: work out number of full splits from the total run time and the split distance. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: number of full splits is what the Splits calculator works out, and it gets there from the total run time, the split distance and the final run time. It is built for a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Splits calculator work?
sections.html:
The Splits calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of full splits in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the total run time, the split distance and the final run time.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in hours / minutes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in meters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in seconds. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: The formula behind the Splits calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of full splits=rounded down, (running distance ÷ split distance)
Split time=pace × split distance
Final run distance=running distance − split distance × rounded down, (running distance ÷ split distance)
Pace=final run time ÷ (running distance − split distance × rounded down, (running distance ÷ split distance))
Running distance=total run time ÷ pace
Split time=(-remaining time + total run time) ÷ split number

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in minutes / seconds, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in minutes per kilometer, and convertible to any of the 20 units on that chip.
  • Shown in meters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.
  • Shown in hours / minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in meters
  • Run pace, opening in minutes per kilometer
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Time, opening in minutes / seconds
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Time, opening in seconds
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Splits calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total run time, the split distance and the final run time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Splits calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of full splits, derived from the total run time, the split distance and the final run time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Splits calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total run time, the split distance and the final run time, which is 4 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter running distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Running distance opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Splits calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
